extracted.intended_audience: literate public and polite society (readers of The Spectator); parents, householders, and general readers seeking moral/social advice
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral and social essays (The Spectator) offering practical guidance on personal behaviour, domestic life, rhetoric, charity, and amusements for the early-18th-century polite reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue should be accompanied by knowledge of the world
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtuous person who lacks a competent knowledge of the world becomes ridiculous in many circumstances and may discredit their best actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid naive simplicity: the author uses the anecdote of St. Francis mistaking a lover's kiss for charity to illustrate how innocence without worldly experience may lead to error. The papers aim to present vice without false allurements and to give virtuous/innocent readers insight into the ways of men so they may avoid snares, corruptions, and prejudiced reasonings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of these papers: inform without vitiating
rubrics_metrics.description: Essays should represent human nature in its changeable colours to open minds without corrupting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write so the virtuous and innocent may 'know in speculation' what they cannot by practice, enabling them to avoid craft and vice. Present vice plainly (not alluringly) while giving practical insight into social behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose innocent, domestic pastimes for families
rubrics_metrics.description: Evening diversions recommended for families should be innocent, practised within doors, and suitable for wives and daughters who read the papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gambling and morally dubious games (the writer explicitly excludes Whisk, Lanterloo, and One-and-Thirty). Recommended indoor amusements include Hot-Cockles, Questions and Commands, Mottoes, Similes, Cross-Purposes, and social games like Blind-Man's Buff; prefer games that provide mirth and exercise without corrupting morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria and examples for consolations of absent lovers
rubrics_metrics.description: Tokens and small keepsakes serve as consolations to lovers separated by absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional remedies include a crooked shilling, a cut crown-piece preserved in halves, heart figures in stone or metal, or personal items (e.g., a mistress's hair plaited in a ring) — the author recommends the ring with plaited hair as especially effective from personal experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infant nursing: mothers ought to nurse their own children when able
rubrics_metrics.description: Mothers who are able should nurse their own infants rather than turning them over to hired nurses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments given: nurses often bring coarse/diseased milk, poor temper or habits which the child may 'imbibe', and nursing by the mother preserves health (prevents vapours, miscarriages), strengthens the mother, and yields stronger children. Exceptions only in rare, real necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of a wet-nurse: health, temper, and circumstances matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If a nurse must be employed, she should not be chosen from mere necessity or poverty without regard to her health, mind, or morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid nurses who are unhealthy, distressed by an ill husband, of poor diet, or motivated solely by money; such conditions can yield bad milk and harmful temperaments in the child. The common answer 'she must live' is flagged as a poor justification for hiring an unsuitable nurse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nurse's influence on child's temperament and health
rubrics_metrics.description: A child's disposition and even diseases can be influenced by the nurse's humours and habits via her milk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites classical and historical examples (Romulus and Remus, Nero, Caligula) to argue that nurses' passions—anger, malice, melancholy, fear—can be transmitted; warns parents that illnesses like rickets, consumptions, or fits may be caused or aggravated by a nurse's condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female eloquence: praise and correction of loquacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Women are naturally talented in eloquence and discourse; such talent should be refined rather than suppressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than discouraging women's speech, aim to cure its disagreeable notes — anger, censoriousness, gossip, and coquetry — and tune it with good-nature, truth, discretion, and sincerity. The essay categorizes female speakers (stirring up the passions, censorious, gossips, coquets) to show where refinement is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public speaking and advocacy: women could excel in rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of rhetoric is highly suitable to women; if admitted, women might advance eloquence in public fora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author suggests the universities might consider women professors of rhetoric and argues that women often display fluency and inventive elocution; this is framed as praise with a call for tempering excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ridicule and laughter: when appropriate and when vicious
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and ridicule can be a relief to the mind, but turning others into an object of ridicule is usually a fault of small, ungenerous tempers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ridicule should aim to correct vice and folly, not to attack what is solemn, decent, or praiseworthy. Avoid fixating on a person's infirmities to gain vulgar applause. The author distinguishes comedy (ridicule by drawing characters as they are) from burlesque (representing persons unlike themselves) and advises choosing the appropriate mode and verse (heroic vs doggerel) depending on whether one elevates or degrades the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral worth measured by beneficence and self-denial
rubrics_metrics.description: True superiority in the esteem of mankind arises from being beneficial to society; self-denial is the foundation of civil virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anyone above mere poverty has opportunities for generous acts; modest persons who deny themselves to relieve others deserve heroic praise. Examples: private generosity (restoring an estate, lending money to save a trader) is lauded as true greatness; public station imposes an obligation to exert talents for public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic beneficence counts as heroic action
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic virtue is not limited to grand public exploits; people in low stations can perform deeds worthy of high esteem through self-denial and assistance to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage recording familial acts of generosity as valuable traditions; small, well-placed acts of charity (saving a merchant, helping a neighbour) are more laudable than mere pursuit of pleasure or gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essay style: favour looseness and freedom when subject is novel
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing a subject not previously treated, the author prefers to assemble reflections loosely and freely rather than in rigid order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essayistic mode permits digression and a free arrangement of thoughts to capture the 'looseness and freedom of an Essay' rather than the strict regularity of a formal discourse.
